- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.11) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast peak values by 1–3%.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >+5% from prior 5-day avg), model often overshoots; cap forecast at 1–2% above recent high or adjust downward if sentiment turns neutral/negative.
- If sentiment shows repeated negative spikes (e.g., -0.22 or -0.28), model underestimates; raise forecast by 1–2% to counteract sentiment-driven downside bias.
- Model tends to lag in early horizon (e.g., 1–3 days ahead) when sentiment is volatile; adjust forecast upward by 0.5–1.5% for short-term (1–3 day) horizons if sentiment is positive.
- For 10+ day horizons, model often fails to capture mean reversion; if sentiment is neutral or slightly positive, apply a 0.5–1.5% downward bias to avoid overconfidence in continuation.
- If sentiment is flat or mildly negative (0.00–0.11) and price is rising, model often underestimates; add 0.5–1.5% to forecast to account for sentiment inertia.
- Avoid forecasting sharp downward moves unless sentiment is clearly negative (e.g., -0.28+ for 3+ consecutive days); if sentiment is neutral, model tends to overcorrect downward.
